C001035.text:
This week, I was proud to announce $65 million in funding to replace our state’s aging rural infrastructure through the Competitive Highway Bridge Program (CHBP) – a grant program I helped create in 2018 to fund highway bridge replacement and rehabilitation projects on roads that serve rural communities. Maine will receive 16 percent of the $408 million awarded nationally through the CHBP this cycle.

The funding will support 15 projects across our state, including 11 bridge replacements across seven counties and four bridge deck replacements on I-95 in Penobscot County. Many of these bridges are more than 50 years old and have exceeded their original design life, creating safety risks for the drivers who rely on them every day. Replacing them is a critical effort that will make travel safer, create jobs, and better connect rural communities across Maine to the rest of our state and nation.

Projects include:

Caratunk (Main St.) – built in 1922, crossing Pleasant Pond Stream

Caratunk (Pleasant Pond Rd.) – built in 1945, crossing Pleasant Pond Stream

Carmel (Fuller Rd.) – built in 1963, crossing Harvey Brook

Chesterville (Mace Rd.) – built in 1950, crossing McGurdy Stream

Cornville (Huff Rd.) – built in 1936, crossing Wesserunsett Stream

Embden (Kennebec River Rd.) – built in 1934, crossing Martin Stream

Lisbon/Bowdoin line (Burrough Rd.) – built in 1936, crossing the Little River

Orland (Bald Mountain Rd.) – built in 1951, crossing Moosehorn Creek

Salem Township (Howard Rd.) – built in 1974, crossing the West Branch Carrabasset River

Sangerville (Silvers Mills Rd.) – built in 1954, crossing French Mills Brook

Topsham (Cathance Rd.) – built in 1920, crossing the Cathance River

Howland (I-95 NB and SB) – bridge decks to be replaced over the Piscataquis River

Old Town (I-95 NB and SB) – bridge decks to be replaced over Pushaw Stream

The President’s Budget Request is just that, a request. To compensate for years of underfunding, the Administration proposes to increase defense funding significantly and recognizes the annual appropriations process as the best way to provide additional funds. The request for just one DDG-51, the workhorse of the U.S. Navy, is insufficient to counter the ever-growing Chinese fleet, which now exceeds the size of the American Navy, as well as other global threats.  
 
While there are some improvements over last year’s domestic discretionary budget request, including full support for the Pell Grant program, the request has several shortcomings. For example, the proposal includes unwarranted funding cuts in biomedical research.  It would also terminate worthwhile programs like LIHEAP, which helps low-income families and seniors to pay their energy bills during the cold winter and hot summer months, and TRIO, which assists low-income, first-generation students in pursuing higher education.  Job Corps, which helps students from troubled backgrounds gain the skills and education they need to enter the workforce, join the military, or pursue higher education, would also be phased out.  These are proven programs that I strongly support.
 
Another program that is important to rural America’s economy is the Essential Air Service program.  The Administration is proposing deep cuts in the EAS program.    
 
After careful review, Congress decisively rejected these particular cuts last year.
 
While the Administration proposes a budget, Congress holds the power of the purse. The Senate Appropriations Committee will now hold hearings with cabinet members and agency heads to review these recommendations and to explore other fiscally responsible proposals.  I hope my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, who too often worked over the last year to impede the appropriations process and shut down federal agencies, will abandon their harmful tactics and work with us to govern responsibly.

Last week, I participated in a U.S. House Appropriations subcommittee hearing with the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director, Scott Kupor as part of my regular oversight duties.

I asked Director Kupor about funding for federal election observers, as stipulated by the Voting Rights Act, which report on election discrimination and report it to the U.S. Department of Justice. Additionally, as a co-chair of the Congressional Military Families Caucus, I asked how OPM is ensuring reasonable accommodations for military spouses employed by the federal government. Finally, I asked about how OPM is working to reduce the growing backlog of federal worker retirement benefit claims. I appreciated hearing from Director Kupor and look forward to following up with him on these and other concerns.

When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

Today, I issued the following statement in response to President Donald Trump’s threat against Iran that “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”

“President Trump launched his war against Iran promising to liberate its 93 million people from a tyrannical regime. Today, he threatened to annihilate them. The President is struggling after plunging the United States into a war without any strategy or clear objectives—and he is now recklessly threatening to commit atrocities and war crimes. It is cruel and a stain on our nation.

“This is unhinged saber rattling that follows consistent threats over the past week to violate international law. The President is using the might of the United States military to wage war without constitutionally mandated approval from Congress.

“Until Congress reasserts itself as a co-equal branch of government, he will remain unchecked and the security of our nation will continue to be at risk.

“At every step in this unconstitutional war, President Trump has made the situation more dangerous and Americans less safe. A key aim of the war is now to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a humiliating loss since the war is the reason the strait is closed to begin with. The President has not adequately explained why Americans are fighting and dying as reasons shift and threats continue to escalate.

“Enough is enough. This war must end and we must repair the self-inflicted damage to our nation’s credibility, economy, and readiness to defend itself. Congressional leadership must act now, and turn to a chapter of diplomacy that can move this troubled region and our world forward.”

RT by @JerryMoran: Took a quick trip yesterday from @NASA_Johnson to visit with Senator @JerryMoran.

For those who have never been to the Cosmosphere in Kansas, this museum and education center is exceptional. To look at the Apollo 13 command module and Jim Lovell’s suit as the Artemis II crew surpassed the distance record was very impactful. I was standing next to Apollo Flight Director Gerry Griffin, and had it not been for his decision-making, and that of his NASA Mission Control team, the Odyssey command module and Jim Lovell’s suit might not have been in the museum to display.

The Cosmosphere has an incredible collection of space hardware, including the Liberty Bell 7 capsule, a full Apollo-Soyuz Test Project mockup, and a Voskhod 2 with the Volga inflatable airlock used by Alexei Leonov during the first spacewalk. You can see how challenging it was, which is one reason he had to partially deflate his suit to get back inside.

We also visited the manufacturers contributing to America’s space program and met the students--the future pilots, astronauts, and engineers who will continue American leadership in space.

Thanks again for the wonderful visit, Senator.

I was grateful to host Administrator Isaacman in Kansas yesterday to visit @the_cosmosphere and cut the ribbon on the Hall of Space Museum. We stopped to view the Apollo 13 capsule, which is housed at the Cosmosphere, just hours before the Artemis II astronauts broke the Apollo 13 record for traveling the farthest away from Earth.

From Hutchinson, we traveled to meet with two local aerospace companies that helped contribute to the construction and success of the Artemis Program – D-J Engineering in Augusta and Globe Engineering Co. in Wichita. The administrator also took time to meet with other aerospace suppliers and pilots-in-training at @wsutech’s National Center for Aviation Training.

The road to space runs through Kansas, and I want to thank Administrator Isaacman for visiting Kansas. Thank you to Cosmosphere CEO Jim Remar, D-J Engineering CEO Rezaul Chowdhury, and Globe Engineering President Jeff Teague for welcoming Administrator Isaacman.

.@GlyphosateGirl says it best: Giving corporate interests a liability shield, especially when their products make people sick, is completely un-American.

RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

W000809.text: Yesterday in Siloam Springs, I had the chance to tour Gates Corporation’s manufacturing facility where industrial and automotive belts are produced. While I was there, we discussed the current supply chain pressures affecting their industry and opportunities for growth.

It is always a pleasure to sit down with the next generation of leaders in Fort Smith who are dedicated to fostering economic development across the city. With these leaders at the helm, I have no doubt that Fort Smith will be well-equipped to succeed in the coming years.

This morning, I toured the River Valley Communications Center (RVCC) where 911 operators work around the clock to ensure that Sebastian County residents have access to vital emergency services. I was grateful to meet some of these hard-working dispatchers today. Though they often work behind the scenes, their work is essential to the safety and security of the community.

I also heard from RVCC Director Wes Milam about some of the challenges that the center is facing as they work to improve the county’s emergency response.

I enjoyed touring Action, Inc. in Barling, where I got a behind-the-scenes look at their operations as one of the largest mechanical contractors in the state. During our visit, we also discussed how Biden-era policies have affected their work on major projects in the Third District and more.

This afternoon, I spoke to a political science class at John Brown University where I shared how our government’s legislative and executive branches interact and how that relationship has evolved over my time in Congress. These students are curious and well-informed, and I was grateful to have this thoughtful conversation with them.

While I was there, I stopped by the re-opening of the Mabee Learning Resource Center. I was even one of the first to try a cup of coffee at the student-run coffee shop, Ground Floor, on their first day open.

James Colangelo is a Navy veteran. In 1985, Mr. Colangelo served on the USS Dale when a compartment on board flooded. He went to the flooded area to survey the damage. Mr. Colangelo became trapped in the tight space as it filled with seawater and fuel, leaving him completely submerged. He nearly drowned but survived. The incident left him with lifelong post-traumatic stress disorder as he continues to relive the terrifying day more than 40 years later.
Because of the incident, Mr. Colangelo filed a claim for disability benefits with the Department of Veterans Affairs but faced challenges. My staff contacted the VA and through my team’s hard work, the VA moved his disability rating to 100% giving him full coverage for his medical costs. Each week, we share stories of people whose lives leave a permanent imprint on our community. This week, we honor one of those rare individuals whose presence made our corner of the world better, stronger, and more connected: Art Younglove of Bristol Borough and Levittown, whom we sadly lost earlier this year after a courageous battle with cancer.

Art was a giant among men in every sense—kind, warm, generous, whip-smart, talented, and utterly one of a kind. But what stayed with you most was something even greater: he was a truly good man.

A proud United States Army veteran and Rohm and Haas employee for more than four decades, Art lived a life grounded in duty, humility, and service. But for so many across our community, he was known most of all as the steadfast Adjutant of Robert Bracken American Legion Post 382 and the heart and soul of the Bracken Cavaliers Drum and Bugle Corps.

If you grew up in Bucks County, as I did, chances are you saw them, heard them before you saw them, or maybe even marched alongside them. The Bracken legacy is not just part of our history—it is part of our identity. And Art was one of its great caretakers.

He carried that legacy forward with extraordinary pride and devotion, helping guide the Corps into its 100th year and playing a leading role in orchestrating its centennial celebration. He also helped bring to life the remarkable mural that now stands in Historic Bristol Borough in tribute to this special organization and all it has meant to generations of families in our community. Art understood something important: history does not live on through stone and paint alone. It lives on in the people who protect it, the traditions that bind us together, and the hometown pride that reminds us who we are.

Yesterday, Art would have turned 87 years old. So today, we gathered with his family and friends at the Bristol Borough Veterans Memorial—a place that meant so much to him—to honor a man who meant so much to so many.

Art was a patriot, steward of tradition, and builder of community,  who gave of himself quietly and generously, and in doing so helped preserve not only an institution, but a spirit of pride, belonging, and connection that will live on far beyond him.

Please join me in extending our deepest condolences to his wife, Grace; his children, Leeann, Catherine, and James; his sisters, Helen and Mary; and all who knew and loved him.

For his service to our nation, his devotion to our community, and the legacy he leaves behind, Art will always be remembered as a true Hometown Hero. 🇺🇸

Spent yesterday on Molokaʻi, and I’m carrying a deep sense of gratitude and urgency with me today.

Across the island—from Kamalāula to Kapaʻakea and all the way out to the East End—I saw neighbors showing up for neighbors. State and County crews were working to clear debris and culverts, preparing for the next round of storms this week.

I heard firsthand about homes flooding and streams overflowing. I talked with homestead leaders who shared their frustrations and hope that something will finally get done to prevent this kind of flooding from happening again. I watched county crews working to repair sunken graves at Kapaʻakea cemetery. And on the east side, I saw crumbling roadways that could cut entire communities off if we don’t act.

We have a lot of work ahead. We must help our homesteads and communities recover—but we also have to rebuild stronger and smarter.

Those who’ve lived on Molokaʻi for generations know exactly how and where the water flows, how to prevent soil loss, and how to protect our reefs from runoff. That knowledge matters. We need to invest in it, listen to it, and build with it.

Because the storms aren’t waiting—and neither can we.

For 47 years, the Iranian regime built an apparatus of death and destruction — exporting terror through proxies like Hamas, Hezbollah, and Houthi militants. Their campaign has killed Americans, allies, and innocents across the Middle East and the world. An Iran with nuclear weapons is a threat to everyone.

Operation EPIC FURY delivered where decades of false promises failed. Iran's nuclear infrastructure and ballistic missile arsenal are destroyed. The regime's proxy networks are degraded. Exactly one month ago, I joined the families of Sgt. Declan Coady and Maj. Jeffrey O'Brien at Dover for the dignified transfer of their remains back to American soil. As a combat veteran and deployed dad who's fought in wars that became endless conflicts, I remain clear-eyed that this operation must not become another one.

A President must have the authority to act decisively in defense of the nation, consistent with the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution. This operation met that standard to stop Iran. This was achieved with overwhelming force.

I am heartened by the ceasefire. Now the mission shifts to securing a lasting agreement that ensures Iran can never threaten the world with a nuclear weapon again.

America's resolve is unmatched. But I have stood with the families who bear the cost of war, and I have fought in wars that lost their way. America is strongest when we fight with clear purpose, defined limits, and the moral conviction to match our firepower.

May God continue to bless our nation and our troops.

M001224.text:
The United States of America must always be prepared to use overwhelming military force when necessary to defend our national security interests and protect Americans at home and abroad. 

And, a President should have the latitude to make decisions to that end, but only to the extent that those decisions are also consistent with the inherent authority of a Commander-in-Chief under the U. S. Constitution and the provisions of the War Powers Resolution. To date, I have supported the President’s decisions relating to the Iranian conflict because they were consistent with these authorities and the ultimate goal of protecting national security interests. 

At the same time, what sets America apart is not only our strength, but how we use it. Our nation has always conducted military operations for just causes and through just and moral means. This must continue in the future; otherwise we forfeit our legitimacy to lead the world. 

So, let me be clear: I do not support the destruction of a "whole civilization." That is not who we are, and it is not consistent with the principles that have long guided America. 

I have and will continue to support a strong national defense—one that is focused, disciplined, and firmly rooted in protecting the safety and security of the American people. But, how we protect the lives of the innocent is just as important as how we engage the enemy. 

America is great because America is good.

⏰ NASA’s estimated timeline of key moments during the lunar fly-by: 

2:45 p.m.: Lunar observations begin. 
6:45 p.m.: During “Earthset,” Earth will glide behind the Moon from Orion’s perspective.
7:02 p.m.: Orion reaches its closest approach to the Moon at 4,070 miles above the surface.
7:07 p.m.: Crew reach their maximum distance from Earth during the mission.
7:25 p.m.: “Earthrise” marks Earth coming back into view on the opposite edge of the Moon. 
8:35-9:32 p.m.: During a solar eclipse, the Sun will pass behind the Moon from the crew’s perspective.
9:20 p.m.: Lunar observations conclude.

ਸ਼੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ਼ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਜੀ ਦੇ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਪੁਰਬ ਦੇ ਪਵਿੱਤਰ ਦਿਹਾੜੇ 'ਤੇ, ਮੈਂ ਸਾਡੀ ਸਭਿਅਤਾ ਦੀ ਇੱਕ ਮਹਾਨ ਅਧਿਆਤਮਿਕ ਸ਼ਖ਼ਸੀਅਤ ਨੂੰ ਸਤਿਕਾਰ ਸਹਿਤ ਸ਼ਰਧਾਂਜਲੀ ਭੇਟ ਕਰਦਾ ਹਾਂ। ਉਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਦਾ ਜੀਵਨ ਨਿਡਰਤਾ, ਕੁਰਬਾਨੀ ਅਤੇ ਮਨੁੱਖਤਾ ਪ੍ਰਤੀ ਡੂੰਘੀ ਚਿੰਤਾ ਦੀ ਇੱਕ ਰੋਸ਼ਨ ਮਿਸਾਲ ਹੈ। ਉਹ ਬੇਅੰਤ ਮੁਸੀਬਤਾਂ ਦੇ ਬਾਵਜੂਦ ਸੱਚ, ਮਾਣ-ਸਨਮਾਨ ਅਤੇ ਧਰਮ ਦੀ ਰਾਖੀ ਲਈ ਅਟੱਲ ਖੜ੍ਹੇ ਰਹੇ। ਉਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਦਾ ਸਦੀਵੀ ਸੰਦੇਸ਼ ਸਾਨੂੰ ਇੱਕ ਨਿਆਂਪੂਰਨ, ਦਿਆਲੂ ਅਤੇ ਸਦਭਾਵਨਾ ਵਾਲੇ ਸਮਾਜ ਦੀ ਸਿਰਜਣਾ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਮਾਰਗ-ਦਰਸ਼ਨ ਕਰਦਾ ਰਹੇ।
